summary:
AstroEnergy PSUT developed Lunar Colony, a playable 3D mission simulator that puts young learners in charge of a lunar outpost. Players manage limited power and supplies, venture outside through an airlock, and collect light readings to decide where to place solar equipment. When a solar particle alert arrives, they must choose between taking shelter immediately and spending time, power, and parts to protect more of the habitat. The drill draws on a historical event recorded in NASA’s Space Weather Database.

Lunar Colony addresses the Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer challenge by making engineering trade-offs something learners can experience firsthand. Players see the consequences of their choices, replay from the same starting point, and explain what they would do differently. That makes space science an entry point into systems engineering and gives educators a concrete way to discuss how evidence, limited resources, and safety shape real decisions.
details:
Lunar Colony is a playable 3D mission simulator developed by AstroEnergy PSUT for the Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer challenge. Players take command of a lunar outpost and make decisions about power, life support, and crew safety with limited time and supplies. They can cycle an airlock, collect light readings at exposed and shaded locations, and use those readings to reason about where to place solar equipment.

The solar particle drill shows how decisions change the outcome. The player can enter a small refuge immediately and conserve parts, or spend parts and keep critical power running while preparing protection for a larger area. Both strategies succeeded in recorded game runs. Staying in an ordinary room reached the exercise’s failure limit. Players can replay from the same checkpoint to compare the strategies and explain what they would do differently.

The drill draws on a historical solar particle event recorded by NASA DONKI on May 10, 2024. The in-game science guide also presents radiation measurements from Artemis I and an ISS lettuce study. These sources give players real examples to investigate, while the drill’s countdown and exposure score are designed for gameplay. NASA DONKI · NASA RadLab · NASA OSDR lettuce study

We built the Windows game in Unreal Engine 5.8 using C++ for the simulation and gameplay, Unreal Motion Graphics for the interface, and Python for test automation. OpenAI Codex assisted development and documentation. Kokoro synthesized selected narration and radio dialogue.

Our goal is to give young learners an engaging first experience with systems engineering and give educators a scenario they can discuss and replay with students. We considered how much information to show at once, how to make failure understandable, and how to connect each decision to visible consequences. In a future school or youth-center pilot, we would ask learners to make a decision in a new scenario and explain it by identifying a constraint, citing evidence, and predicting a consequence.
